title: Washback in Depth — Designing Tests That Teach Well

pts: Unit 21 introduced washback as a concept to recognise; this poster addresses actively designing for positive washback.
A test's format, content and stakes all shape what happens in the classroom leading up to it, whether intended or not.
Designing with washback in mind means asking, before anything else, what teaching behaviour this test will encourage.

v: One recent test paper you or your school set

items: Before looking at any item in detail, write one sentence answering: ‘If learners prepared only for this test, what would they practise?’
Go through the paper and list the skills and behaviours each section rewards.
Compare that list with the aims of the course or scheme of work (Unit 14).
Classify the likely washback: positive, negative or mixed; strong or weak; narrow or broad.
Write the ‘washback question’ at the top of your next test-planning sheet, so that it comes first.
Do the task with a previous year’s board paper and a class you are preparing for it.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

blocks.x: One teacher’s analysis of a Class 9 English half-yearly paper (written for this book):

lines: Section A: unseen passage with short questions → rewards reading for detail; good.
Section B: letter to the principal, fixed format → rewards memorizing the layout; little attention to purpose or reader.
Section C: textbook questions answered from guidebooks → rewards memorizing model answers.
No speaking or listening component → these skills will be squeezed out of preparation.

blocks.x: Asking first what the test will encourage turns washback from a side-effect into a design aim (Alderson and Wall 1993).

body: Purpose: to show washback flowing back from a test. Content: a timeline of weeks leading to a test paper at the right; arrows curve back from the test into the classroom weeks, labelled ‘what gets taught’ and ‘how it gets taught’. Style: clean diagram. Board version: a line with a box at the end and curved arrows back.

items: Google Docs (free) with comments for annotating a test paper with colleagues.

blocks.x: A photocopied paper annotated in the margins in a staff meeting.

pts: A multiple-choice-only test predictably encourages multiple-choice-style teaching, regardless of the skill it claims to assess.
A test including genuine task-based, communicative components encourages that kind of classroom practice in preparation.
This connects directly to Unit 46's rubric design — test format is itself a curriculum-shaping decision.

v: Three versions of a test of the same skill, in different formats

items: Prepare three ways of testing the same outcome, for example ‘can write a complaint email’: (a) multiple-choice items about email conventions; (b) error correction in a model email; (c) writing an email to a given situation, scored with a rubric (Unit 46).
In groups, teachers describe the preparation lessons each format would probably produce.
Compare what learners would be able to do after each kind of preparation.
Choose, or combine, formats with the washback you want.
Repeat for speaking: a read-aloud task, a picture description, and a paired role-play.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

lines: Multiple choice → lessons of rule lists and practice items; learners may never write a complete email.
Error correction → proofreading practice; useful but narrow.
Task with rubric → lessons that model, draft and give feedback on real emails; learners practise the target skill.

blocks.x: Test format is a curriculum decision. The task version asks more of the marker; hence the rubric work of Unit 46.

body: Purpose: to show that format shapes practice. Content: three moulds labelled ‘MCQ’, ‘error correction’ and ‘task’; clay pressed into each comes out a different shape, labelled with the classroom activity it produces. Style: simple, visual metaphor. Board version: three boxes with arrows to three activities.

items: Google Forms (free) to show teachers how easily an MCQ test is built, and to discuss what that ease encourages.

blocks.x: Three paper versions of the test laid side by side.

pts: A test covering only a narrow slice of the intended curriculum risks teaching narrowing to match it — 'teaching to the test' in its negative sense.
Broad, representative sampling across a test's content reduces this risk without needing to test everything exhaustively.
This is a design decision with real curriculum-wide consequences, not a minor technical detail.

v: Scheme of work; a test blueprint template

items: List the course outcomes for the term across the four skills, vocabulary, grammar and discourse.
Build a blueprint (specification) grid: outcomes in rows; weightings and item types in columns.
Check coverage: does every major outcome appear somewhere, even with a small weighting?
Plan to vary which minor outcomes are tested from year to year, so that none can be safely skipped.
Share the blueprint with colleagues who set parallel papers.
Map the last three years’ papers against the syllabus to see what has never been tested.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

blocks.x: Part of a blueprint for a Class 11 term test (written for this book):

lines: Reading for gist and detail (unseen texts): 25%
Writing a genre taught this term (report or article): 25%
Speaking (paired discussion, assessed in class): 15%
Listening (short recorded talk): 10%
Vocabulary and grammar in context: 15%
Literature: response to an unseen short poem: 10%

blocks.x: When a test samples only a narrow slice of the curriculum, teaching tends to narrow to match it (Wall and Alderson 1993). Broad, representative sampling reduces the risk without testing everything.

body: Purpose: to show a test specification as a map of the curriculum. Content: a grid with outcomes in rows and item types in columns; shaded cells show what is tested, with a few unshaded cells flagged for next year. Style: tidy, technical. Board version: a table with ticks.

items: Google Sheets or Microsoft Excel (free online version) for a blueprint grid with weighting totals.

blocks.x: A blueprint table on squared paper kept in the department file.

points.sub: How much is riding on this
pts: Higher-stakes tests produce stronger washback effects, for better or worse, than low-stakes ones.
Consider deliberately whether a given assessment point needs to be high-stakes, given the washback that comes with that choice.
This connects to Unit 42's argument for distributing assessment weight across a portfolio rather than one high-stakes event.

v: The school’s assessment calendar and weightings

items: List every assessment point in the year and its weight in the final record.
Mark each as high, medium or low stakes from the learners’ point of view.
Ask for each high-stakes point: does it need to be high-stakes, and what washback will that produce?
Consider moving some weight to a portfolio or to several smaller tasks (Unit 42).
Propose one change to the department.
Ask learners to rate the stakes of each assessment and compare their view with the official weights.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

lines: A: The final exam is 80 per cent. No wonder the last month is all revision guides.
B: What if speaking and a writing portfolio together counted for 30 per cent, spread across the year?
A: Then they’d be worth practising all year, not just in March.

blocks.x: Higher stakes produce stronger washback, for better or worse (Bailey 1996). Spreading weight distributes attention across the year.

body: Purpose: to show stakes as a force on teaching. Content: a balance scale with one heavy exam block on one side, and on the other a set of smaller blocks labelled ‘portfolio’, ‘speaking task’ and ‘project’. Style: clear. Board version: a see-saw with labelled boxes.

items: Google Sheets (free) to model how changes in weighting affect final scores.

blocks.x: The assessment calendar redrawn on chart paper with weights shown as bar lengths.

pts: Pilot a new test's likely washback by observing preparatory teaching in a trial run before full deployment.
This is a specialist step rarely taken with informally-designed classroom tests, but standard practice for high-stakes ones.
Piloting catches unintended washback effects — a test that quietly rewards memorisation over genuine skill, for instance.

v: A new or revised test; a short observation sheet

items: Share the draft test with a colleague two or three weeks before a trial.
Ask them to prepare one class for it as they normally would, without special instructions.
Observe one preparation lesson, or ask them to keep a short log of what they did.
Interview three or four learners briefly: ‘How did you prepare?’
Compare preparation with the intended washback and revise the test.
In a single-teacher school, pilot with a colleague at a cluster resource centre or DIET.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

blocks.x: A pilot finding (written for this book):

lines: Intended: learners practise summarizing an unseen talk.
Observed: the teacher found that last year’s talks were on the school website; learners memorized summaries.
Revision: use new talks each year and assess the summary with a rubric focused on main ideas, not memorized wording.

blocks.x: Piloting is standard practice for high-stakes examinations (Green 2007) but rarely done with classroom tests. Even a small pilot catches memorization of predictable content.

body: Purpose: to show piloting as a check before full use. Content: a small test paper being tried with a few learners in the corner of a classroom, with a magnifying glass over their preparation notes. Style: realistic. Board version: a small box labelled ‘pilot’ with an arrow to a large box labelled ‘use’.

items: Google Forms (free) for a two-minute learner survey on how they prepared.

blocks.x: A half-page observation sheet and four short learner interviews noted by hand.

pts: Teachers preparing learners for a test benefit from understanding its intended washback, not just its format.
Without this understanding, teaching can default to narrow test-format drilling even when the test itself was designed more broadly.
This connects to Unit 46's principle of sharing rubric criteria transparently, applied at the level of whole-test design intent.

v: Teacher activity; also for teacher educators
A test; a one-page ‘intent note’ template

items: For each section of the test, write one sentence on what it is meant to encourage in the classroom.
Add one example of good preparation and one of poor preparation.
Attach the note to the test specification when it is shared with colleagues.
In a department meeting or DIET session, discuss the note before discussing the test items.
Collect questions and revise the note.
Write a version for learners: ‘How to prepare well for this test.’
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

blocks.x: An intent note for a speaking section (written for this book):

lines: Section: paired discussion on a topic from the term’s themes.
Intended washback: regular pair and group discussion; practice in agreeing, disagreeing and building on a partner’s point (Unit 39).
Good preparation: weekly short discussions with peer feedback.
Poor preparation: memorizing opening speeches on likely topics.

blocks.x: Wall (2005) found that teachers need to understand the intentions behind a new examination, not only its format, if it is to change practice.

body: Figure 57.6 A note that travels with the test

Purpose: to show design intent accompanying a test. Content: a test paper clipped to a smaller note headed ‘Why this test looks like this’, passed from one teacher to another. Style: warm, simple. Board version: two rectangles joined by a paper clip.

items: Google Drive (free) shared folder in which each test is stored with its intent note.

blocks.x: The intent note printed on the back of the teacher’s copy of the test.

points.h: Washback in High-Stakes vs. Classroom Testing
pts: Large-scale exams (Cambridge, IELTS) and a teacher's own end-of-unit test both carry washback, at very different scales.
The same design principles apply at both scales — a teacher designing a unit test is doing washback design too, just smaller.
This reframes everyday classroom test-writing as a genuinely specialist skill worth this level of deliberate attention.

v: Public information on one international exam (e.g. IELTS or Cambridge C1 Advanced); one of your own unit tests

items: Read the official description of one section of an international exam and note its intended washback.
Describe how coaching centres commonly prepare candidates for it, from your own experience.
Apply the same questions to your own unit test: format, sampling, stakes and communication.
Identify one principle used in the large exam that you can adapt, and one pitfall you want to avoid.
Compare a state board paper with a central board paper for the same class.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

lines: Large exam, speaking: paired or face-to-face tasks with trained examiners and published descriptors → encourages speaking practice, but also memorized ‘templates’ in some coaching.
My unit test: no speaking at all → encourages no speaking practice.
Adapt: a short paired speaking task with public descriptors. Avoid: predictable topics that invite memorized answers.

blocks.x: A teacher writing a unit test is doing washback design too, on a smaller scale (Hughes 2003).

body: Figure 57.7 A big wave and a ripple

Purpose: to show washback at two scales. Content: a large wave labelled ‘board and international exams’ and a small ripple labelled ‘my unit test’, both moving towards the same shore labelled ‘classroom practice’. Style: simple, graphic. Board version: a large and a small curve pointing to one line.

items: Official exam websites, such as IELTS and Cambridge English (free public information and sample papers).

blocks.x: Printed sample tasks from a published practice book.

points.h: Revising a Test for Better Washback
pts: Treat a test's washback as something to observe and revise, following Unit 9's reflective-practice cycle applied to assessment design.
A test producing unwanted preparatory behaviour is a design signal to revise, not evidence that teachers are 'teaching to the test' improperly.
This closes the loop: washback design, like teaching itself, improves through deliberate iteration.

items: After a test, collect evidence of how learners prepared (a quick survey or three short interviews).
Compare that with the intended washback in your intent note.
Identify one unintended effect.
Change one design feature to address it (format, sampling, stakes or communication).
Record the change and the reason in the test file, and check the effect next time.
Keep a department ‘washback log’ in which all revisions are recorded over several years.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

blocks.x: A washback log entry (written for this book):

lines: Unintended effect: learners memorized three model essays and adapted them to any question.
Design change: essay prompts now require the use of data from a short table given in the paper.
Check next year: do learners practise interpreting data and building an argument from it?

blocks.x: Unwanted preparation is a design signal, not simply evidence that teachers are ‘teaching to the test’. This is the reflective cycle of Unit 9 applied to assessment design.

body: Purpose: to show washback design as iterative. Content: a cycle of four stages: ‘design with washback in mind’, ‘pilot’, ‘observe preparation’ and ‘revise’, with a test paper at the centre that changes slightly at each turn. Style: clean. Board version: a circle with four labels.

items: Google Sheets (free) for a running washback log.

blocks.x: A washback log kept in the department assessment file.

body: Take one end-of-unit test you will use this term. Write an intent note for it, share it with one colleague, and survey five learners afterwards about how they prepared. Change one feature of the test before you use it again, and record why.

dek: Unit 57 of 100: moving from understanding washback (Tier I) to deliberately engineering a test's backward effect on teaching to be positive rather than distorting.

aims.x: Most teachers spend their careers administering tests that someone else designed. Yet every teacher who writes an end-of-unit test, a term examination or a question paper for the school is also shaping what happens in the weeks before it. This unit treats that influence, washback, as something to design for. It moves from recognizing washback, as in Unit 21, to engineering it so that preparing for a test becomes good preparation for using English.
By the end of this unit you should be able to:

items: explain washback and its main dimensions: direction, intensity and scope;
predict the classroom behaviour that a given test format is likely to encourage;
sample test content broadly enough to avoid narrowing the curriculum;
decide deliberately how much weight an assessment point should carry;
pilot a classroom test for its likely washback before using it widely;
communicate the intended washback of a test to the teachers who prepare learners for it;
revise a test in the light of evidence about how teachers and learners prepared for it.

why: Why this matters. Most teachers only ever administer tests someone else designed. Designing one is a different, specialist skill — and one with real power to shape a whole course.

background.x: The term washback (or backwash, as Hughes (2003) calls it) refers to the effect of a test on teaching and learning. It was long assumed that good tests automatically produce good teaching. Charles Alderson and Dianne Wall (1993) challenged this assumption. In a paper that is still widely cited, they asked whether washback exists at all, and proposed a set of hypotheses about what a test might affect: what teachers teach, how they teach, what learners learn, and at what rate and depth. Their point was that washback must be investigated, not assumed.

Wall’s own research made the investigation concrete. In a study of a new English examination in Sri Lanka, designed partly to encourage communicative teaching, Wall and Alderson (1993) found that the examination did change the content of teaching, but did far less to change methods. Teachers focused on the parts of the textbook that looked like the exam, and taught them in familiar ways. Wall (2005) later argued that introducing a new test is an educational innovation, and that like any innovation it succeeds only when teachers understand it, have the materials and training to act on it, and work in a system that supports the change. Samuel Messick (1996) placed washback within the broader idea of validity: a test that leads to harmful teaching has consequences that count against it. Kathleen Bailey (1996) and the collection edited by Cheng, Watanabe and Curtis (2004) show that washback varies with the stakes, the context and the people involved.

In India, washback is a daily reality. Board examinations at the end of Classes 10 and 12, and competitive entrance examinations, strongly shape what happens in classrooms. Where a board English paper rewards memorized answers about prescribed lessons and fixed-format letters, teaching tends to follow. NEP 2020 names this problem directly, calling for board examinations to test core capacities and competencies rather than months of coaching and memorization, and for a national assessment centre, PARAKH, to set norms (Ministry of Human Resource Development 2020). NCF 2023 likewise asks that assessment support learning and test competencies rather than rote recall (NCERT 2023). These are washback aims. This unit gives classroom teachers, heads of department and teacher educators the tools to pursue them at their own scale.

items: Washback analysis. A written analysis of one existing test, predicting its washback and comparing it with course aims.
Test blueprint. A specification grid showing broad sampling and a justified weighting.
Pilot report. Brief notes on a washback pilot with one colleague, and the changes made in response.
Intent note and log. An intent note for one test and a washback log entry after it has been used.
Which test that you administer has the strongest effect on your teaching? Is that effect one you would choose?
What skills have disappeared from your classroom because they are not tested?
Which of your assessment points could carry less weight without loss?
How could you find out how your learners actually prepare for your tests?
What would teachers in your school need, besides a new test, to change how they teach?

Sample material from IELTS, Cambridge English or Indian examination boards must not be reproduced without permission; refer readers to the official websites instead. Screenshots of Google Forms, Sheets or Drive require permission or replacement with original illustrations.

terms.def: The aspect of validity concerned with the social consequences of test use, including its effects on teaching and learning (Messick 1989).
The choice of which parts of a syllabus a test includes; broad, representative sampling reduces the risk that teaching narrows to match the test.
The tendency for teaching to focus only on what is tested, leaving out other valuable content and skills, such as speaking, when an examination tests only reading and writing.
A short document attached to a test specification that explains what each section is meant to encourage in the classroom, with examples of good and poor preparation, to promote positive washback.
Trying out new materials or a test with a small group before full use, in order to identify problems and revise them.

The beneficial effect of a test on teaching and learning, for example when including a speaking component in a school examination encourages teachers to give learners regular speaking practice in class.

The importance of a test’s consequences for the people involved. High-stakes tests, such as board examinations, affect futures and so tend to produce stronger washback than low-stakes classroom quizzes.
Narrowing teaching to the content and formats of an examination, often at the expense of wider language skills. It is a common form of negative washback in high-stakes systems.

A document setting out what a test measures and how, including its purpose, test takers, content, task types, marking and weighting. It guides test writers and helps ensure consistency across versions.

The effect of a test on teaching and learning, which may be positive or negative (Alderson and Wall 1993). Board examinations that test only reading and writing often lead to neglect of listening and speaking.
